claim: Central insulin is critically involved in the regulation of hedonic feeding.
source: Central insulin is critically involved in the regulation of hedonic feeding.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about insulin's role in feeding regulation.

claim: Insulin resistance in overweight has recently been shown to reduce the inhibitory function of insulin in the human brain.
source: Insulin resistance in overweight has recently been shown to reduce the inhibitory function of insulin in the human brain.
evidence: This statement references recent research findings without specific citations in this sentence.

claim: Older people are highly vulnerable to hyperinsulinemia.
source: How this relates to effective weight management is unclear, especially in older people, who are highly vulnerable to hyperinsulinemia and in whom neural target systems of insulin action undergo age-related changes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about aging and metabolic function.

claim: Neural target systems of insulin action undergo age-related changes in older people.
source: How this relates to effective weight management is unclear, especially in older people, who are highly vulnerable to hyperinsulinemia and in whom neural target systems of insulin action undergo age-related changes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about aging effects on neural systems.

claim: 50 overweight, non-diabetic older adults participated in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, pharmacological functional magnetic resonance imaging study.
source: Here, 50 overweight, non-diabetic older adults participated in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, pharmacological functional magnetic resonance imaging study before and after randomization to a 3-month caloric restriction or active waiting group.
evidence: This describes the study design and sample size.

claim: Treatment outcome in dieters can be predicted by baseline measures of individual intranasal insulin inhibition of value signals in the ventral tegmental area related to sweet food liking.
source: Our data show that treatment outcome in dieters can be predicted by baseline measures of individual intranasal insulin (INI) inhibition of value signals in the ventral tegmental area related to sweet food liking as well as, independently, by peripheral insulin sensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Treatment outcome in dieters can be predicted independently by peripheral insulin sensitivity.
source: Our data show that treatment outcome in dieters can be predicted by baseline measures of individual intranasal insulin (INI) inhibition of value signals in the ventral tegmental area related to sweet food liking as well as, independently, by peripheral insulin sensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: INI inhibition of hedonic value signals in the nucleus accumbens improved with weight loss at follow-up.
source: At follow-up, both INI inhibition of hedonic value signals in the nucleus accumbens and peripheral insulin sensitivity improved with weight loss.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the follow-up measurements.

claim: Peripheral insulin sensitivity improved with weight loss at follow-up.
source: At follow-up, both INI inhibition of hedonic value signals in the nucleus accumbens and peripheral insulin sensitivity improved with weight loss.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the follow-up measurements.

claim: Neural insulin function can be improved by weight loss even in older age.
source: These data highlight the critical role of central insulin function in mesolimbic systems for weight management in humans and directly demonstrate that neural insulin function can be improved by weight loss even in older age, which may be essential for preventing metabolic disorders in later life.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The prevalence of overweight and obesity rises dramatically with age.
source: The prevalence of overweight and obesity rises dramatically with age and is associated with increased morbidity and reduced quality of life (Kalyani et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kalyani et al., 2017.

claim: Overweight and obesity are associated with increased morbidity and reduced quality of life.
source: The prevalence of overweight and obesity rises dramatically with age and is associated with increased morbidity and reduced quality of life (Kalyani et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kalyani et al., 2017.

claim: Hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance are potential causes and consequences of obesity.
source: Hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance are potential causes and consequences of obesity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance are negatively affected by age.
source: Both are negatively affected by age and both play a pivotal role for the development of type 2 diabetes and other age-related diseases (Palmer and Kirkland, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Palmer and Kirkland, 2016.

claim: Hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance play a pivotal role for the development of type 2 diabetes and other age-related diseases.
source: Both are negatively affected by age and both play a pivotal role for the development of type 2 diabetes and other age-related diseases (Palmer and Kirkland, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Palmer and Kirkland, 2016.

claim: It has long been assumed that insulin resistance in aging precedes the development of hyperinsulinemia.
source: For instance, it has long been assumed that insulin resistance in aging precedes the development of hyperinsulinemia, while recent data suggest a reverse direction (Janssen, 2021).
evidence: This describes a historical assumption in the field, with citation to Janssen, 2021 for the contrasting view.

claim: Recent data suggest that hyperinsulinemia precedes insulin resistance in aging.
source: For instance, it has long been assumed that insulin resistance in aging precedes the development of hyperinsulinemia, while recent data suggest a reverse direction (Janssen, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Janssen, 2021.

claim: There is evidence from animal and human research of a weight-independent effect of aging on insulin sensitivity.
source: Moreover, there is evidence from animal and human research of an weight-independent effect of aging on insulin sensitivity (Ehrhardt et al., 2019; Petersen et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ehrhardt et al., 2019 and Petersen et al., 2003.

claim: Central insulin mediates non-homeostatic feeding for pleasure by signaling within mesolimbic reward circuits.
source: Findings in rodents and humans indicate that, apart from signaling in hypothalamic neurocircuits regulating energy homeostasis, central insulin mediates non-homeostatic feeding for pleasure by signaling within mesolimbic reward circuits (Davis et al., 2010; Murray et al., 2014; Tiedemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Davis et al., 2010; Murray et al., 2014; Tiedemann et al., 2017.

claim: Insulin action in the ventral tegmental area reduces hedonic feeding in rodents.
source: Specifically, insulin action in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) reduces hedonic feeding in rodents (Labouèbe et al., 2013; Mebel et al., 2012) and decreases hedonic value signals in the VTA and nucleus accumbens (NAc) in lean subjects (Tiedemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Labouèbe et al., 2013 and Mebel et al., 2012.

claim: Insulin decreases hedonic value signals in the VTA and nucleus accumbens in lean subjects.
source: Specifically, insulin action in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) reduces hedonic feeding in rodents (Labouèbe et al., 2013; Mebel et al., 2012) and decreases hedonic value signals in the VTA and nucleus accumbens (NAc) in lean subjects (Tiedemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tiedemann et al., 2017.

claim: Insulin-mediated long-term depression of VTA dopamine neurons is reduced in hyperinsulinemia.
source: On the other hand, insulin-mediated long-term depression of VTA dopamine neurons is reduced in hyperinsulinemia (Liu et al., 2013) and aberrant insulin action in VTA–NAc pathways has been observed in insulin-resistant participants (Tiedemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2013.

claim: Aberrant insulin action in VTA–NAc pathways has been observed in insulin-resistant participants.
source: On the other hand, insulin-mediated long-term depression of VTA dopamine neurons is reduced in hyperinsulinemia (Liu et al., 2013) and aberrant insulin action in VTA–NAc pathways has been observed in insulin-resistant participants (Tiedemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tiedemann et al., 2017.

claim: Improvement of hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance, as achieved by caloric restriction, is key in the prevention and treatment of obesity, type 2 diabetes, or cardiovascular diseases in aging.
source: There is consensus that the improvement of hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance, as achieved by caloric restriction (CR), is key in the prevention and treatment of obesity, type 2 diabetes, or cardiovascular diseases in aging (Janssen, 2021; Ryan, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Janssen, 2021 and Ryan, 2000.

claim: Evidence from human studies for effects of caloric restriction on central nervous insulin signaling are sparse.
source: Evidence from human studies for such effects, however, are sparse, especially when it comes to central nervous insulin signaling.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of research literature.

claim: High insulin sensitivity in MEG theta activity was predictive for long-term weight management in 15 young adults.
source: High insulin sensitivity in MEG theta activity was predictive for long-term weight management in 15 young adults (Kullmann et al., 2020b) suggesting the critical role of central insulin action for future feeding regulation and as a major target of treatment intervention.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kullmann et al., 2020b.

claim: Changes in function and distribution of adipose tissue can trigger metabolic alterations such as hyperinsulinemia.
source: Whether such intervention can modulate brain insulin sensitivity in older age is particularly questionable given that changes in function and distribution of adipose tissue can trigger metabolic alterations such as hyperinsulinemia (Palmer and Kirkland, 2016; Tchkonia et al., 2010) and relevant brain circuits for central insulin action like the dopaminergic mesolimbic pathway undergo age-related changes (Karrer et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Palmer and Kirkland, 2016 and Tchkonia et al., 2010.

claim: The dopaminergic mesolimbic pathway undergoes age-related changes.
source: Whether such intervention can modulate brain insulin sensitivity in older age is particularly questionable given that changes in function and distribution of adipose tissue can trigger metabolic alterations such as hyperinsulinemia (Palmer and Kirkland, 2016; Tchkonia et al., 2010) and relevant brain circuits for central insulin action like the dopaminergic mesolimbic pathway undergo age-related changes (Karrer et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Karrer et al., 2017.

claim: Fifty older (>55 years) overweight, non-diabetic individuals were randomly assigned to a 3-month caloric restriction intervention or an active waiting group.
source: Fifty older (>55 years) overweight, non-diabetic individuals were randomly assigned to a 3-month, CR intervention or an active waiting group (WG).
evidence: This describes the study design and participant allocation.

claim: Participants rated the palatability of high and low sugar food pictures and the attractiveness of non-food items after receiving intranasal insulin or placebo.
source: Before and after the intervention, overnight fasted participants took part in a crossover, placebo-controlled, double-blind pharmacological fMRI examination in which they rated the palatability of high and low sugar food pictures and the attractiveness of non-food items (control) after receiving intranasal insulin (INI) or placebo.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Fasting c-peptides and blood glucose were assessed to calculate peripheral insulin sensitivity.
source: Fasting c-peptides and blood glucose were assessed to calculate peripheral insulin sensitivity.
evidence: This describes the measurement methods used in the study.

claim: The study sample consisted of 50 overweight and obese older adults with mean age 63.7 ± 5.9 years and mean BMI 32.7 ± 4.3 kg/m².
source: Fifty overweight and obese older adults (age: 63.7 ± 5.9 years, range 55–78 years; body mass index [BMI]: 32.7 ± 4.3 kg/m², range 25.8–32.4 kg/m²; 20 men) with an explicit wish to lose weight participated in this study.
evidence: This provides demographic data for the study sample.

claim: 30 participants underwent a 3-month caloric restriction diet (diet group) and 20 participants were assigned to a 3-month active waiting group.
source: Of these, 30 randomly selected participants underwent a 3-month CR diet (diet group, DG, 14 men), while 20 participants were randomly assigned to a 3-month active WG (6 men).
evidence: This describes the group allocation in the study.

claim: Normal HbA1C values confirm the exclusion of manifest diabetes in the study participants.
source: Normal HbA1C values confirm the exclusion of manifest diabetes in overweight and obese participants who are at risk for T2D but in whom elevated insulin release may still compensate for reduced insulin sensitivity (mean HOMA-2: 2.2 ± 0.08, range 1.2–3.5).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HbA1C measurement data.

claim: The diet group showed a significant mean weight loss of 3.61 kg after 3 months.
source: After 3 months (mean 96 ± 10 days, no group differences: p = 0.91), follow-up measurements showed a significant mean weight loss compared to baseline of 3.61 kg (±3.06, T(29) = 6.47, p < 0.001, d = 1.18) in the DG, reflecting on average a 4% loss of baseline bodyweight and BMI, respectively (T(29) = 6.66, p < 0.001, d = 1.22).
evidence: This is a primary outcome measure with statistical analysis.

claim: The diet group showed on average a 4% loss of baseline bodyweight and BMI after 3 months.
source: After 3 months (mean 96 ± 10 days, no group differences: p = 0.91), follow-up measurements showed a significant mean weight loss compared to baseline of 3.61 kg (±3.06, T(29) = 6.47, p < 0.001, d = 1.18) in the DG, reflecting on average a 4% loss of baseline bodyweight and BMI, respectively (T(29) = 6.66, p < 0.001, d = 1.22).
evidence: This is a primary outcome measure with statistical analysis.

claim: Twenty-one dieters (70%) lost more than 2 kg.
source: Twenty-one dieters (70%) lost more than 2 kg (range: 2.5–9.6 kg), only one dieter gained more than 0.4 kg (3.1 kg).
evidence: This provides descriptive statistics on weight loss outcomes.

claim: In the waiting group, mean weight change was 0.07 kg.
source: In the WG, mean weight change was 0.07 kg (±1.5 kg).
evidence: This provides descriptive statistics on weight change in the control group.

claim: Percentage BMI change differed significantly between diet and waiting groups (p < 0.001).
source: Accordingly, percentage BMI change differed significantly between groups (BMI%change: both T(48) = 5.45, p < 0.001, d = 1.39; Figure 2, Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between groups, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Higher insulin sensitivity at baseline predicted more subsequent weight loss in dieters (r = −0.37; p = 0.046).
source: To test the predictive value of baseline insulin resistance in the periphery for dietary success after 3 months, we correlated individual HOMA-2 scores assessed on the placebo session from T0 with BMI%change in dieters and found a significant correlation (r = −0.37; p = 0.046, n = 30, Pearson's correlation). That is, higher insulin sensitivity at baseline predicted more subsequent weight loss in dieters (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis with statistical significance, with reference to Figure 3a.

claim: No correlation was observed between BMI%change and baseline BMI.
source: Control analyses showed no such correlation in the WG and no correlation was observed between BMI%change and baseline BMI (all p > 0.16).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing no significant relationship.

claim: Food items were liked significantly more than non-food items at baseline placebo session (all p < 0.001).
source: As expected, in the T0 placebo session, food items were liked significantly more than non-food items on the categorical (yes/no) and parametric (cumulated ratings 1–8) level (all p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the task with statistical analysis.

claim: Higher insulin sensitivity was related to lower high sugar food liking (r = 0.38; p = 0.006).
source: C-peptide-based insulin sensitivity was correlated with HS liking, in a way that higher insulin sensitivity was related to lower HS liking (r = 0.38; p = 0.006; n = 50, Pearson's correlation, Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis with statistical significance.

claim: Analysis on sugar-specific values (HS > LS) demonstrated a significant two-way interaction session × BMI%change (F(1,48) = 6.24; p = 0.016).
source: While there was no interaction with insulin effects on general food versus non-food values, analysis on sugar-specific values (HS > LS) demonstrated a significant two-way interaction session × BMI%change (F(1,48) = 6.24; p = 0.016, ƞ² = 0.12, rmANCOVA).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from rmANCOVA.

claim: In participants with a minimum BMI reduction of 1%, insulin decreased sugar preference at baseline significantly (T(24) = 2.10; p = 0.046).
source: To further explore this finding, the analysis of insulin effects was limited to participants with a minimum BMI reduction of 1% (n = 25). In this subsample, insulin decreased sugar preference (i.e., percentage of sweet foods in preferred foods) at baseline significantly (T(24) = 2.10; p = 0.046, n = 25, d = 0.42, t-test) and this effect could not be explained by BMI or HOMA-2 (all p > 0.12).
evidence: This is a subgroup analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Food compared to non-food items in the placebo session at baseline yielded highly significant activations in a network of reward-related brain regions including the bilateral insula, medial OFC, and amygdala.
source: As expected from our previous study (Tiedemann et al., 2017), the analysis of differences in BOLD responses to food compared to non-food items in the placebo session at T0 yielded highly significant activations across all participants in a network of reward-related brain regions including the bilateral insula, medial OFC, and amygdala (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is an fMRI analysis result with reference to Figure 4a and comparison to previous work.

claim: Regions that encode the subjective value of items comprised regions of the brain's valuation network including the vmPFC and NAc.
source: Also in line with our previous findings, regions that encode the subjective value of items, that is, regions that show a positive correlation between the amplitude of the BOLD response and subjective preference values, comprised regions of the brain's valuation network including the vmPFC and NAc (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is an fMRI analysis result with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: Valuation of high sugar compared to low sugar food items evoked significantly stronger correlations between BOLD signal and preference values in the ACC/vmPFC, right caudate nucleus and thalamus (all p < 0.05 FWE corrected).
source: Furthermore, valuation of HS compared to LS food items evoked significantly stronger correlations between BOLD signal and preference values in the ACC/vmPFC (Figure 4c), the right caudate nucleus and thalamus (all p < 0.05 FWE corrected) and as trend in the right NAc (9, 10, −7; FWE = 0.09, Figure 4c).
evidence: This is an fMRI analysis result with statistical correction, with reference to Figure 4c.

claim: Participants in whom INI reduced the high sugar-specific valuation signal in the midbrain at baseline are more likely to benefit from caloric restriction by weight loss at follow-up.
source: Simple regression analysis including BMI%change as a covariate yielded insulin-induced signal changes in the left VTA to predict subsequent weight loss across all participants as well as within subjects from the DG alone (−8, −13, −13, p < 0.05 FWE corrected; Figure 3b). Results in the left VTA were still significant when including age and BMI as covariates in the analysis (p < 0.05 FWE corrected). This indicates that participants in whom INI reduced the HS-specific valuation signal in the midbrain at T0 are more likely to benefit from CR by weight loss as assessed at T1.
evidence: This is an fMRI regression analysis result with statistical correction, with reference to Figure 3b.

claim: Peripheral and central insulin sensitivity at baseline have an independent positive impact on subsequent weight loss in overweight older dieters.
source: Within participants from the DG, this model turned out to be highly significant (F(2,27) = 10.07; adjusted R² = 0.39; p < 0.001), with both predictor variables explaining substantial variability (VTA-Bold: β = 0.54; T = 3.70; p < 0.001; HOMA-2: β = −0.35; T = 2.41; p = 0.023, p < 0.025 Bonferroni corrected). Inclusion of BMI in a control model demonstrate these effects not to be driven by baseline bodyweight (Appendix 1—table 3). This indicates, that peripheral and central insulin sensitivity at baseline have an independent positive impact on subsequent weight loss in overweight older dieters.
evidence: This is a multiple regression analysis result with statistical testing.

claim: HOMA-2 scores were significantly improved at follow-up within participants from the diet group (T(29) = 2.33; p = 0.027).
source: Within participants from the DG, HOMA-2 scores were significantly improved at follow-up (T(29) = 2.33; p = 0.027, d = 0.43).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of HOMA-2 scores before and after intervention.

claim: The improvement in HOMA-2 scores was directly correlated with successful weight change within dieters (r = 0.43; p = 0.017).
source: Moreover, the improvement in HOMA-2 scores was directly correlated with successful weight change within dieters (r = 0.43; p = 0.017; N = 30, Pearson's correlation) and across all participants (r = 0.33; p = 0.020; N = 50, Pearson's correlation, Figure 5).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis with statistical significance, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Participants from the diet group showed a significantly reduced sweet food preference under insulin compared to placebo at follow-up (T(29) = 2.59; p = 0.015).
source: In behavior, participants from the DG showed a significantly reduced sweet food preference (i.e., percentage of sweet foods in preferred foods) under insulin compared to placebo at follow-up (T(29) = 2.59; p = 0.015, d = 0.47) that tended to be stronger compared to the WG (T(49) = 1.80; p = 0.08) and to baseline (T(29) = 1.67; p = 0.11) (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a behavioral analysis result with statistical testing, with reference to Figure 6a.

claim: Behavioral insulin effects in the diet group at follow-up were reflected by a stronger reduction of sugar-specific value signals in the NAc under insulin in the diet group compared to the waiting group (peak right: 10, 8, −7, p = 0.028 FWE corrected and peak left: −10, 12, −8, p = 0.043 FWE corrected).
source: On the neural level, behavioral insulin effects in the DG at follow-up were reflected by a stronger reduction of sugar-specific value signals in the NAc under insulin in the DG compared to the WG (peak right: 10, 8, −7, p = 0.028 FWE corrected and peak left: −10, 12, −8, p = 0.043 FWE corrected, t-test).
evidence: This is an fMRI analysis result with statistical correction.

claim: The effect in the right NAc was significantly stronger when directly comparing follow-up to baseline valuation responses between groups (peak: 10, 8, −6, p = 0.019 FWE corrected).
source: The effect in the right NAc was also significantly stronger when directly comparing follow-up to baseline valuation responses between groups (peak: 10, 8, −6, p = 0.019 FWE corrected; two-sample t-test).
evidence: This is an fMRI analysis result with statistical correction.

claim: Improvement of insulin sensitivity measured in the blood correlated with increased insulin effects in the NAc (peak left: −10, 10, −7, p = 0.03 FWE corrected).
source: To this end, changes in HOMA-2 scores (post > pre) were entered as a covariate in a simple regression of BOLD signals from the contrast HS > LSPL>IN_post > HS > LSPL>IN_pre within participants from the DG. Results revealed positive correlations between improvement of insulin sensitivity measured in the blood and increased insulin effects in the NAc (peak left: −10, 10, −7, p = 0.03 FWE corrected; peak right: 10, 10, −7; Figure 7).
evidence: This is an fMRI regression analysis result with statistical correction, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: Peripheral and central markers of insulin sensitivity were low at baseline in overweight and obese individuals.
source: As was expected from overweight and obese individuals, both peripheral and central markers of insulin sensitivity were low at baseline and both selectively improved with weight loss after CR in dieters.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the baseline measurements.

claim: Both peripheral and central markers of insulin sensitivity selectively improved with weight loss after caloric restriction in dieters.
source: As was expected from overweight and obese individuals, both peripheral and central markers of insulin sensitivity were low at baseline and both selectively improved with weight loss after CR in dieters.
evidence: This is a summary of the longitudinal findings.

claim: Participants with higher hyperinsulinemia demonstrated a specifically enhanced sugar preference at baseline.
source: At baseline, participants with higher hyperinsulinemia demonstrated a specifically enhanced sugar preference which fits animal and human data on the critical role of sugar-enriched diets on whole-body insulin functioning (Macdonald, 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from baseline data with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Baseline insulin markers in the blood were not related to behavioral or neural INI responses to high sugar items.
source: Baseline insulin markers in the blood, however, were not related to behavioral or neural INI responses to HS items.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analyses.

claim: Attenuated insulin transport into the cerebrospinal fluid in individuals with reduced whole-body insulin sensitivity might explain the lack of central insulin effects across participants at baseline.
source: This may be driven by the general lack of central insulin effects across participants at baseline which fits with data in overweight younger adults (Tiedemann et al., 2017) and which might result from an attenuated insulin transport into the cerebrospinal fluid in individuals with reduced whole-body insulin sensitivity (Heni et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Pathophysiological changes due to overweight and aging might at least in part independently affect peripheral and central insulin effects.
source: This indicates that, even though peripheral insulin might be a good proxy for central insulin functioning in younger lean adults (Tiedemann et al., 2017), pathophysiological changes due to overweight and aging might at least in part independently affect peripheral and central insulin effects.
evidence: This is an inference from the study findings with citation to previous work.

claim: The impact of the predictive values of insulin sensitivity could not be explained by body mass.
source: The impact of these predictive values could not be explained by body mass, which demonstrates that insulin sensitivity, but not necessarily obesity, is predictive for future weight management.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regression analysis results.

claim: The VTA plays a central role in the insulinergic modulation of hedonic eating behavior.
source: The VTA plays a central role in the insulinergic modulation of hedonic eating behavior (Labouèbe et al., 2013; Mebel et al., 2012; Tiedemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Direct administration of insulin into the VTA reduces hedonic feeding and depresses somatodendritic DA in the VTA.
source: Direct administration of insulin into the VTA reduces hedonic feeding and depresses somatodendritic DA in the VTA which has been attributed to the upregulation of the number or function of DA transporter in the VTA (Mebel et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mebel et al., 2012.

claim: INI can suppress food value signals in the mesolimbic pathway by negatively modulating projections from the VTA to the NAc.
source: Connectivity analyses of fMRI data further suggest that INI can suppress food value signals in the mesolimbic pathway by negatively modulating projections from the VTA to the NAc (Tiedemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tiedemann et al., 2017.

claim: Insulinergic effects at baseline and follow-up were specifically restricted to high sugar food stimuli.
source: Insulinergic effects at baseline and follow-up were specifically restricted to HS food stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The palatability of sugar has been linked to DA release in the NAc in rodents.
source: The palatability of sugar has been linked to DA release in the NAc in rodents (Hajnal et al., 2004) and there is evidence for neural adaptations in the NAc in response to excessive sugar intake (Klenowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hajnal et al., 2004.

claim: There is evidence for neural adaptations in the NAc in response to excessive sugar intake.
source: The palatability of sugar has been linked to DA release in the NAc in rodents (Hajnal et al., 2004) and there is evidence for neural adaptations in the NAc in response to excessive sugar intake (Klenowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Klenowski et al., 2016.

claim: Higher sugar preference in overweight individuals has been related to stronger white matter connectivity within the VTA–NAc pathway.
source: For instance, higher sugar preference in overweight individuals has been related to stronger white matter connectivity within the VTA–NAc pathway (Francke et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Francke et al., 2019.

claim: Insulinergic functionality in the VTA-NAc network may be critical for hedonic feeding regulation as the reduction of sugar intake is substantial for the success of a dietary intervention.
source: Our data indicate that insulinergic functionality in this network may be critical for hedonic feeding regulation as the reduction of sugar intake is substantial for the success of a dietary intervention.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: A reduced insulinergic functionality of the VTA-NAc network in older overweight individuals may result from adiposity.
source: A reduced insulinergic functionality of this network in older overweight individuals may not only be the consequence of adiposity (Mattson and Arumugam, 2018) but may also result from age-related metabolic and neural changes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Aging is associated with a decrease of cortical insulin concentration, reduced insulin receptor binding ability and reduced insulin transport across the blood–brain barrier.
source: Aging is associated with a decrease of cortical insulin concentration, reduced insulin receptor binding ability and reduced insulin transport across the blood–brain barrier (Cholerton et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cholerton et al., 2011.

claim: Target systems of metabolic–hedonic networks relevant for insulin action undergo age-related changes.
source: Moreover, target systems of metabolic–hedonic networks relevant for insulin action undergo age-related changes (Mattson and Arumugam, 2018; Smith et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mattson and Arumugam, 2018 and Smith et al., 2020.

claim: The dopamine system is particularly vulnerable to aging which might lead to functional changes in subcortical reward circuits.
source: The dopamine system, for example, is particularly vulnerable to aging which might lead to functional changes in subcortical reward circuits (Dreher et al., 2008; Karrer et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dreher et al., 2008 and Karrer et al., 2017.

claim: There is a significant loss of dopaminergic neurons in the basal ganglia including the VTA with aging.
source: There is a significant loss of dopaminergic neurons in the basal ganglia including the VTA (Siddiqi et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Siddiqi et al., 1999.

claim: Insulin acts via glutamatergic synaptic transmission onto VTA DA neurons.
source: Given that insulin acts via glutamatergic synaptic transmission onto VTA DA neurons (Labouèbe et al., 2013) this might have direct consequences on the insulinergic suppression of subsequent DA release in mesolimbic regions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Labouèbe et al., 2013.

claim: Chronic metabolic morbidities like obesity can further accelerate brain aging.
source: For instance, chronic metabolic morbidities like obesity can further accelerate brain aging (Mattson and Arumugam, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mattson and Arumugam, 2018.

claim: A chronic positive energy balance adversely affects brain function.
source: A chronic positive energy balance thereby adversely affect brain function (Beyer et al., 2017) and structure (Janowitz et al., 2015) and is related to many of the cellular and molecular hallmarks of brain aging such as oxidative damage and neuroinflammation (Mattson and Arumugam, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Beyer et al., 2017, Janowitz et al., 2015, and Mattson and Arumugam, 2018.

claim: While there was no association between blood parameters and central insulin action at baseline, weight-change related improvements in peripheral and central insulin sensitivity were directly correlated at follow-up.
source: Intriguingly, while there was no association between blood parameters and central insulin action at baseline, weight-change related improvements in peripheral and central insulin sensitivity in our sample of older dieters were directly correlated at follow-up, indicating a common modulator.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings with interpretation.

claim: Changes in central insulin sensitivity were restricted to an increased inhibition of value signals in the NAc but not the VTA.
source: Moreover, changes in central insulin sensitivity were restricted to an increased inhibition of value signals in the NAc but not the VTA.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI findings.

claim: Weight change specifically normalized adiposity-related dysfunctions while variability due to aging itself were less affected.
source: Thus, one could speculate that weight change specifically normalized adiposity-related dysfunctions while variability due to aging itself were less affected.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Improvement in insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis is a broadly observed metabolic effect of caloric restriction in rodents as well as young and older adults.
source: Improvement in insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis is a broadly observed metabolic effect of CR in rodents (Yu et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021) as well as young and older adults (Fontana and Klein, 2007; Johnson et al., 2016; Most and Redman, 2020; Most et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to research in rodents and humans.

claim: The mechanisms behind caloric restriction effects on insulin sensitivity have been related to significantly increased hepatic insulin clearance.
source: The mechanisms behind these effects are not fully understood yet but have been related to significantly increased hepatic insulin clearance (Bosello et al., 1990), reduced levels of thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP; Johnson et al., 2016), and generally decreased oxidative stress and inflammatory processes (Fontana and Klein, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to relevant research.

claim: Caloric restriction can induce adaptive cellular responses that can enhance neuroplasticity and stress resistance in animals.
source: Animal data about CR effects on brain functioning suggest that CR can induce adaptive cellular responses that can enhance neuroplasticity and stress resistance, for example, by the upregulation of neurotrophic factor signaling, suppression of oxidative stress and inflammation, stabilization of neuronal calcium homeostasis, and stimulation of mitochondrial biogenesis (Mattson, 2012; Mattson and Arumugam, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mattson, 2012 and Mattson and Arumugam, 2018.

claim: Recent work in rodents demonstrates improved insulin sensitivity following caloric restriction that was associated with enhanced brain monoamine concentrations such as increased DA levels in the striatum.
source: In addition, recent work in rodents demonstrate improved insulin sensitivity following CR that was associated with enhanced brain monoamine concentrations such as increased DA levels in the striatum (Portero-Tresserra et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Portero-Tresserra et al., 2020.

claim: The study data extend beneficial neural effects of caloric restriction in animals to improved central insulin functioning in the human brain.
source: Our data extend these beneficial neural effects of CR in animals to improved central insulin functioning in the human brain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in the context of animal research.

claim: Weight-related brain dysfunction is a risk factor for metabolic disorders, cognitive decline and neurodegeneration.
source: This is particularly intriguing with regard to our non-diabetic sample of elderlies, in whom weight-related brain dysfunction is not only a risk factor for metabolic disorders but also for cognitive decline and neurodegeneration (Ekblad et al., 2017; Janssen, 2021; Mattson and Arumugam, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ekblad et al., 2017, Janssen, 2021, and Mattson and Arumugam, 2018.

claim: The study used a dietary intervention that reduced participants' individual caloric intake by 10–15% with a minimal intake set to 1200 kcal per day.
source: We chose a relatively mild dietary intervention that reduced participants' individual caloric intake by 10–15% with a minimal intake set to 1200 kcal per day.
evidence: This describes the intervention protocol.

claim: There was only a mild-to-moderate average weight loss of 4% in the diet group.
source: Accordingly, there was only a mild-to-moderate average weight loss of 4%.
evidence: This is a summary of the weight loss outcome.

claim: Even mild weight change was related to significant improvement of insulin sensitivity in the periphery and in the brain.
source: Even this mild weight change was related to significant improvement of insulin sensitivity in the periphery and in the brain which underline that adiposity-related dysfunctions in later life are able to normalize.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Adiposity-related dysfunctions in later life are able to normalize.
source: Even this mild weight change was related to significant improvement of insulin sensitivity in the periphery and in the brain which underline that adiposity-related dysfunctions in later life are able to normalize.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings.

claim: New evidence suggests hyperinsulinemia precedes insulin resistance.
source: This is especially promising given new evidence for hyperinsulinemia preceding insulin resistance (Janssen, 2021) which makes it a key target for early interventions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Janssen, 2021.

claim: Long-term effects of weight loss are probably particularly dependent on prefrontal mediated psychological strategies including self-control during eating decisions.
source: It is now critical to understand the long-term effects of such changes with a special focus on food intake assuming that long-term effects are probably particularly dependent on prefrontal mediated psychological strategies including self-control during eating decisions (Hare et al., 2009; Phelan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Peripheral insulin sensitivity as well as central hedonic feeding regulation predict and normalize with dietary success in overweight elderlies.
source: In conclusion, we provide data demonstrating that peripheral insulin sensitivity as well as central hedonic feeding regulation predict and normalize with dietary success in overweight elderlies.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main findings.

claim: The independent contribution peripheral and central insulin sensitivity make for successful feeding regulation emphasizes the necessity to control for both when treating individuals at risk for metabolic disorders.
source: Our results of an independent contribution peripheral and central insulin sensitivity make for successful feeding regulation emphasize the necessity to control for both when treating individuals at risk for metabolic disorders.
evidence: This is a clinical implication drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Sixty-four overweight and obese participants (age >55, BMI >25 kg/m²) with an explicit wish to lose weight were recruited for this study.
source: Sixty-four overweight and obese participants (age >55, BMI >25 kg/m²) with an explicit wish to lose weight were recruited for this study.
evidence: This describes the initial recruitment for the study.

claim: Thirty-eight participants were randomized to the dietary intervention group while 26 were randomly assigned to the waiting group.
source: Thirty-eight participants were randomized to the dietary intervention group while 26 were randomly assigned to the WG.
evidence: This describes the initial randomization scheme.

claim: The final sample size was 50 complete datasets (55–78 years, M = 63.7, SD = 5.9, 20 men), 30 from the diet group and 20 from the waiting group.
source: This led to a final sample size of 50 complete datasets (55–78 years, M = 63.7, standard error [SD] = 5.9, 20 men), 30 derived from the DG and 20 derived from the WG.
evidence: This describes the final analyzed sample after exclusions.

claim: Sample sizes were based on previous findings on successful caloric restriction in older adults.
source: Sample sizes were based on previous findings on successful CR in older adults (Witte et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the rationale for sample size with citation.

claim: A dropout rate of 25% was considered in the recruitment scheme.
source: A dropout rate of 25% was considered in our recruitment scheme.
evidence: This describes the study planning considerations.

claim: The study was approved by the local ethics committee of the Ethical Board, Hamburg, Germany.
source: The study was approved by the local ethics committee of the Ethical Board, Hamburg, Germany.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The study has been registered at DRKS (DRKS00028576).
source: The study has been registered at DRKS (DRKS00028576).
evidence: This is a statement about study registration.

claim: Participants received 160 IU of insulin or vehicle by intranasal application.
source: After anthropometric measurements, ratings of feelings of current hunger and collection of blood samples, participants received 160 IU of insulin (Insuman Rapid, 100 IU/ml) or vehicle (0.27% m-Kresol, 1.6% glycerol, and 98.13% water) by intranasal application.
evidence: This describes the experimental intervention.

claim: Participants began the preference paradigm 30 min after the nasal spray was applied to ensure that the insulin had time to take its full effect.
source: Participants began the preference paradigm (in the fMRI scanner) 30 min after the nasal spray was applied; this delay was introduced to ensure that the insulin had time to take its full effect (Born et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the timing of the experimental procedure with citation to Born et al., 2002.

claim: Participants of the diet group received a 12-week professional diet program that consisted of individual nutrition counseling by experienced clinical dieticians and a psychological group intervention.
source: Participants of the DG received a 12-week professional diet program that consisted of (1) individual nutrition counseling by experienced clinical dieticians, who were blinded to the underlying study hypothesis, and (2) a psychological group intervention (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This describes the intervention protocol.

claim: Dieters received an individually planned dietary regimen that reduced each subject's individual caloric intake by 10–15%.
source: Within individual sessions and based on individual dietary records from the previous 7 days, dieters received an individually planned dietary regimen that reduced each subject's individual caloric intake by 10–15%.
evidence: This describes the dietary intervention details.

claim: Minimal caloric intake was set to 1200 kcal per day.
source: Minimal intake was set to 1200 kcal per day.
evidence: This describes the dietary intervention constraint.

claim: The dietary regimen was based on the 10 guidelines of the German Nutrition Society.
source: The regimen was based on the 10 guidelines of the German Nutrition Society (https://www.dge.de/).
evidence: This describes the basis for the dietary intervention.

claim: Participants from the waiting group were instructed to not change previous eating habits during the 3-month period.
source: Participants from the WG were instructed to not change previous eating habits during the 3-month period.
evidence: This describes the control group instructions.

claim: A c-peptide-based index is thought to be a more reliable indicator of insulin secretion that is minimally affected by hepatic insulin clearance, has longer half-life and that is more sensitive to incident T2D.
source: A c-peptide-based index is thought to be a more reliable indicator of insulin secretion that is minimally affected by hepatic insulin clearance, has longer half-life and that is more sensitive to incident T2D (Jones and Hattersley, 2013; Leighton et al., 2017; Okura et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Jones and Hattersley, 2013; Leighton et al., 2017; Okura et al., 2018.

claim: There was a significantly higher within-subject variability in prescan insulin levels at T0 and T1 compared to c-peptide levels.
source: Indeed, in a control analysis we observed a significantly higher within-subject variability (coefficient of variance, COV) in prescan insulin levels at T0 as well as T1 compared to c-peptide levels (T0: T(49) = 4.79; p < 0.001; T1: T(49) = 4.47; p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a control analysis result with statistical testing.

claim: Four sets of stimuli were randomly presented on the four scanning days.
source: Four sets of stimuli were randomly presented on the four scanning days.
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation protocol.

claim: Each stimulus set consisted of 70 food and 70 non-food color images selected from the internet.
source: Each one of the four parallel versions consisted of 70 food and 70 non-food color images selected from the internet.
evidence: This describes the stimulus materials.

claim: The four food sets did not differ in sugar content.
source: The four food sets did not differ in sugar content (see Appendix 1—figure 5 for distribution of sugar content).
evidence: This is a validation result for the stimulus sets.

claim: Validation of all four stimulus sets revealed that the four sets did not differ significantly regarding the mean preference ratings (all p > 0.43).
source: Validation of all four sets was conducted in an independent sample (n = 16) and revealed that the four sets did not differ significantly regarding the mean preference ratings (all p > 0.43).
evidence: This is a validation result for the stimulus sets.

claim: All imaging data were acquired on a Siemens PRISMA 3T scanner using a 32-channel head coil.
source: All imaging data were acquired on a Siemens PRISMA 3T scanner (Erlangen, Germany) using a 32-channel head coil.
evidence: This describes the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Functional data were obtained using a multiband echo-planar imaging sequence.
source: Functional data were obtained using a multiband echo-planar imaging sequence.
evidence: This describes the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Structural and functional data were analyzed using SPM12 and custom scripts in MATLAB.
source: Structural and functional data were analyzed using SPM12 (Welcome Department of Cognitive Neurology, London, UK) and custom scripts in MATLAB.
evidence: This describes the data analysis software.
